title: The Oxidizer Gap — Editor Intro
summary: Opening title splash establishes the Mojave's visible dependence on water infrastructure, Tethergrid's evolution from coordinator to gatekeeper, and Launch-Shop's belief that the open sky offers another route.
settingText: Mojave infrastructure panorama at first light — community water tanks and pipes crossing open desert, distant pumping hardware and a Tetherwell relay structure below an enormous unobstructed sky; Launch-Shop and a small homemade rocket may appear only as distant scale elements.
panelPlan: Full-page prestige editorial composition with no conventional panel grid. Build a spectacular vertical Mojave panorama: water infrastructure and settlement hardware anchor the lower page, long utility lines and a restrained Tethergrid structure occupy the middle distance, and an enormous open sky dominates the upper field.

Use visual scale to make infrastructure feel physical and unavoidable rather than abstract. The desert should look inhabited and maintained, not post-apocalyptic. Water tanks, pipes and equipment are functional; the tension comes from control, not ruin.

Keep Launch-Shop and the homemade rocket small enough that they promise possibility without revealing any Issue 1 action, engineering problem, launch outcome or specific town result. Do not show a rocket in flight.

Reserve generous clean negative-space zones for the unusually long editor text. Treat the prose as deliberate magazine-quality comic typography rather than speech balloons. Use hierarchy to give HOW, WHETHER, THE SKY and the final line extra visual weight without changing the words.
The eye should travel from water hardware at the bottom toward unrestricted sky at the top. The final line should land against the largest area of open sky.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: There are places where infrastructure disappears into the background.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The Mojave is not one of them.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Out here, you can see the pipes crossing the desert. You can see the pumping stations, the relay towers, the power lines and the reservoirs. You can drive for an hour beside the machinery that keeps a settlement alive and never once forget what happens if it stops working.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Water has always been the hard part.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Years ago, Tethergrid helped solve that problem.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Its Tetherwell network connected wells, pumps, storage systems and communities across enormous distances. It measured what was available, decided where it was needed and made sure nobody could simply drain the system dry. In a desert growing hotter and more crowded, that kind of coordination didn't just make sense.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: It saved lives.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Then something changed.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Slowly, the system that decided how water should move also became the system that decided whether it moved at all.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: A broken pump could be repaired.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: A dry well could sometimes be replaced.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: But an authorization?

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: That came from somewhere else.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: And somewhere along the way, people who had spent generations surviving one of the harshest landscapes on Earth found themselves waiting for permission to use the machinery sitting in their own towns.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Arvin, Milo and Lucia have a different idea.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: They travel the Mojave in Launch-Shop, a rolling aerospace workshop full of salvaged engines, old flight hardware, mismatched tools and machines that should probably have been retired years ago.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: They repair things.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: They rebuild things.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: And when the thing a community needs doesn't exist, they have a habit of making one.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Which brings us to a patch of open desert, a homemade rocket, and a problem considerably larger than either of them.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Because Tethergrid controls a remarkable amount of what crosses the Mojave.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The pipes.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The pumps.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The network.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The permissions.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: But above all of it is several hundred kilometers of infrastructure nobody has figured out how to put behind a gate.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The sky.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Welcome to Backyard Rockets.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Unlike the water, nobody owns the sky.

directionInline.text: This is a non-diegetic opening editor/title page, not a literal story scene. Preserve every caption exactly and prioritize flawless legibility despite the long text. It must explain enough of the world for the first story pages to make sense while revealing nothing that happens after the opening situation: do not show Esperanza's result, a successful relay authentication, any nozzle failure or repair, Cyrus's response, or a rocket in flight. The emotional promise is spectacular scale plus practical human defiance, not propaganda or a recap.
